graphite-build-taste-with-ai.title: Graphite Build Taste With AI
graphite-build-taste-with-ai.summary:
Translate your taste profiles into skills embedded in any AI sessions
· Design · Software Engineering

sections.title: Problem Defining
sections.body: "AI slop" is produced everyday from prompts. Taste is not easy to be expressed linguistically, it comes with an accumulated collections from various sources. Hence Graphite's built -- an AI native taste collector that helps to translate your personal preferences into taste profiles other AI tools can understand. So you create unique work instead of average slop.

sections.title: The Canvas
sections.body: Graphite is used as a sketch of your artwork, its rough but with the highest inspiration. Start with an idea and your canvas will have multi-media content populated around your inspiration.

sections.title: The user experience
sections.body: Preview any content and drag into Keep or Release, the algorithm will understand your preference and continuously share inspirational content without being overwhelming. Graphite will learn your taste profile and create a skill that embed taste into any AI sessions.

blocks.caption: content relevant to you will populate automatically
The generated design playbook, export as a skill to any AI tool to keep building

sections.title: The features
sections.body: Features are designed to keep you inspired and creative, as your taste changes the interface UI will change accordingly! Skill playbook curates your skill.md for any AI sessions, Profile shows your visual identity and Command gives you control on the type of media you want...

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body:
I believe creativity is randomized it requires a by chance development of taste to create something create. So dont just build, build something great...

The limitation of this product is its integration with other in the market AI tools, with full integration Graphite should become the AI era of Pinterest where inspirations are translated into creative with ease.

ai-commercial-product.title: AI Commercial Product
ai-commercial-product.summary:
Commercial features shipped @Tiktok Search
· Business Strategy · Engineering 
Visuals are confidential, hence describing my work through text

blocks.html:
[ AI assisted agent translating demand to result directly ]
· pre-launch product design 

Goal: 
increase lead quantity and quality by integrating AI chatbot in users experience

The Design:
AI Chatbot Integration 
Before: Users interested in an ad (ie. car viewing) they have to click into ad and leave a message for the shop owner to reply, the lead devalues as time passes. Leading to low conversion rate. 

After: An Ai assistant appears in search summary and users can chat with an assistant about the ad. Get 247 service and your appointment for car view will be booked directly without human intervention. Saves time for shop owners and increase conversion result. 

Design Decision:
User workflow: entry points for users to be assisted are determined by A/B testings on user interactions to existing icons, maximizing entry point engagement

(Embed AB table)

Engineering Decision:
Personalized conversation: training model to understand users adaptive intent and personalize conversation trajectory to reach final conversion result

[ AI distribute personalized ad content to target users ] 
· launched, completed design and engineering

Goal: 
increase lead conversion rate by personalizing user experience

The Design:
Location Auto Selection Feature
Before: one ad group was bound to a single destination (Website, 1P Form, or DM). Advertisers had to judge for themselves which path performed better, and in practice a given advertiser usually only ever used one.

After: Under the Leads goal, Optimization Location supports multi-select by default; the delivery system automatically picks the best path/component based on user preference.

Results: advv +24%, daily revenue increased from $4k to $39k

Search Design:
a) Query to user intent - creatives
Use query embeddings to understand user intent and serve ads across a more diverse set of ad locations.

[Example: 28 y/o · female · New York · interest tags include "wedding dress, wedding ring" searches "wedding photography New York pricing"]
The model receives (user, query="wedding photography New York pricing", ad)
  • Query intent classification: local-commercial + pricing/decision stage (high purchase intent)
  • (user × query) crossover: interest signals and action signals overlap
  • (query × ad) relevance: strong content relevance to a specific New York wedding photography studio's ad


b) Query to keyword relevancy - model foundation
Search delivery path: the delivery path infers user intent through the query, and weights relevance heavily. Need to improve model performance for an accurate search ecpm scoring.
  • Search eCPM formula: Rank Score = ECPM + HiddenCost (Relevance + UserIntentMismatch)
  • Feed eCPM formula: Rank Score ~ ECPM (bid × pCTR × pCVR × 1000)

drift-rl-on-routing-system.title: Drift
drift-rl-on-routing-system.summary:
A ML trained routing algorithm that helps runners to explore new routes around the city
· Design · Engineering 
Completed as a group of 3, my main role was designing the wearable and software integration

sections.title: Problem Defining
sections.body: Today's routing systems are destination-based -- ie. Google Maps, takes a location and calculates the most efficient route to get there. However the rigid way of commuting is not by our nature. I believe we need an exploratory routing algorithm that can personalize our ways around the city.

sections.title: Prototype outcome
sections.body: Building a wearable that output haptic signals to direct you, opening up your senses to fully immerse in the surrounding environments.

blocks.caption: Paired with software that can personalize your routes interactively

sections.title: Engineering Decision
sections.body: The model is trained on GeoJSON parameters that matter to runners (ie. city landscape, canopy shade, park locations, and similar features.) The costing formula weighs the user's personal interests as top priority, generating routes accordingly. As a result, everyone's route looks different.

sections.title: Design Decision
sections.body: Drift is designed without a screen, an electrical device embedded into fabric worn on the wrist. The goal is to minimize size and weight while preserving functionality, designing a form that lets the user clearly sense actuation, and choosing materials that endure sweat while maximizing comfort.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body: The core aim of Drift was to explore simulating possibilities from a noisy dataset. One limitation: with a small test-user pool, the routing system didn't reach statistically significant precision. Going forward, I intend to dig deeper into integrating ML/RL into simulation training for predictions in other contexts.

sixth-embodied-intelligence.title: Sixth Embodied Intelligence
sixth-embodied-intelligence.summary:
AI on body -- intelligent wearable collect bio-sensing data and give real-time respond
Paper publishing @UbiComp
· Design · Engineering 
Completed as a group of 4, my main role was designing the wearable and software integration

sections.title: Problem Defining
sections.body: LLMs are integrated into our daily lives, but its constrained to our current hardware. What if AI can understand your body and tell you in real time what to do? SIXTH is an attempt to build the thinnest LLM hardware that can reason based on your bio data.

sections.title: Design Decision
sections.body: SIXTH is engineered to conform to the human body while minimizing weight and discomfort. It's designed to feel like a second skin worn over your base layer rather than a separate garment. A layer of conductive fabric tracks vital signs directly at the body, connected by conductive wiring so lightweight it disappears entirely.

blocks.caption: Layered design - using marino wool to ensure comfort and avoid sweat
Wearable design - integrate fashion elements into the clothing

sections.title: Software and Process
sections.body:
The software is designed to accommodate two modes:
Daily mode connects to the cloud, delivering feedback through a digital device. 
Extreme mode relies on locally stored heuristics to make decisions on-device, triggering output signals (like heating or actuation) for immediate feedback.

blocks.caption: Sensing positioning - avoiding under garment to collect accurate data

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body:
SIXTH reflects my interest in embodied intelligence, I believe AI won't just live on our phones or laptops, but will extend our understanding of our own bodies.

However this research is high cost to productize therefore would love to extend my knowledge on manufacturing and brand collaborations to realize research into market.

sections.title: Problem Defining
sections.body: AI slop is contaminating our native instinct as creative beings. Generalized design appear based on rules not 'taste'. How do we capture each individual's uniqueness and help to develop their own taste? GRAPHITE is the answer - its an AI native taste builder which allows your exploration to be painless and transfer the taste you have built throughout time to whichever projects you are working on in AI.

peri-ai-agentic-creator-tool.title: Peri Ai Agentic Creator Tool
peri-ai-agentic-creator-tool.summary:
Agentic negotiator that are in charge of all your deals
· Business · Software Engineering

heroBlocks.caption: The challenge: build an negotiator that can bring better deals than human

sections.title: Problem Defining
sections.body: Creators are being changed >30% from their deals from creative agencies who aren't bringing values, LLMs are not capable of understanding the negotiation context and bring the best value out of your deals

sections.title: market & Solution
sections.body: We charge 10% commission with AI agent providing scalable and personalized end to end service for creators - from sourcing deals to strategic negotiating to the final contracting.

sections.title: Result
sections.body: Achieved users on both creator (eventually 50+ users) and brand side (2 finalized deals)

sections.title: Engineer decision
sections.body:
The key design decision stays in the negotiation layer, to replace the intuition in many human agents

1. Negotiation Policy - designed in tiers for human intervention

Tiers

  • Auto-handle: inside pre-authorization boundary -- allowed category, deliverable terms, standard terms.
  • Escalation: touches an irreversible term (price commit, exclusivity, usage rights) or the extraction confidence is low.

2. Negotiation Simulation

On selecting the move: Simulate each candidate N times against the sampled persona and play out several rounds ahead to predict counter offer.

On selecting the language: Lead with brand's goal. Figure out what the brand actually cares about, then pitch the same deal in those terms.


3. Failure Backup

Action Validation: The system's degraded state is raise to human decision, never a wrong outbound action. Guardrail to protect against a hallucinated commitment to a brand

  • Language Validation: deterministic validator on every outbound message -- floor, banned category, commitment language, PII.

sections.title: Reflection
sections.body: Peri was built and front-deployed with customer in 3weeks, it was my first try on building a to B product and roll out GTM plan facing enterprises. I learnt in depth what D2C brands care about and how to scale a product from 0-1.

michelins-for-ai-benchmark-research.title: Michelins for AI Benchmark Research
michelins-for-ai-benchmark-research.body:
01 · Initial direction

TL;DR

  • Why: We wanted to understand why strong AI evaluation research often fails to reach industry.

  • Key points: The main gaps are visibility, adoption, and interpretation. Interactive tests and expert review can make capability evidence easier to understand and trust.

  • Finding: Useful benchmarks should evaluate the full system around task execution, not only the foundation model.

1. The Model

The first Michelin Guide was published in France in 1900. It listed maps, petrol stations, and other resources intended to encourage motorists to travel farther, wear out their tires, and purchase more.

Over time, the guide developed into a credible restaurant rating system. Anonymous inspectors paid for their own meals and produced independent assessments. What began as marketing became trusted evaluation infrastructure.

2. The Gap

AI research and industry lack a comparable system for discovering, interpreting, and validating evaluation methods. New benchmark and data-pipeline research appears faster than most people can meaningfully assess it.

  • Visibility: Independent research is difficult to discover unless it is continuously maintained, promoted, or associated with a well-known lab.

  • Adoption: Industry teams rarely have enough time to follow every paper or determine which methods matter in their own application context.

  • Interpretation: Benchmark scores describe performance numerically, but many people cannot see what a model can actually do through those numbers alone.

The result is a visibility gap: research with strong institutional reach receives attention, while other useful methods remain difficult to find and evaluate.

3. The Ecosystem

What if evaluating a model were as accessible as playing a game on Steam? Users could interact with capabilities directly, compare how models behave, and discuss the differences through visible evidence.

Expert “inspectors” could then test whether a capability creates value inside a real application. Their extended reviews would document the model, evaluation method, use context, and observed outcome.

This evidence could help industry select models, help users understand capabilities, and give researchers feedback about what deserves further development. Together, these exchanges could form a healthier loop between research, users, and industry.

Current takeaway. Most companies evaluate the foundation model. What matters increasingly is the architecture and systems surrounding task execution. We may need benchmarks that evaluate these systems as a whole.

IDEP · Research notes

Original blog post

arena-ai-competitive-analysis.title: Arena.ai Competitive Analysis
arena-ai-competitive-analysis.body:
02 · Case study

TL;DR

  • Why: We studied Arena to understand how an evaluation method earned industry trust and adoption.

  • Key points: Arena combined direct human comparisons with open access, frequent leaderboard updates, research visibility, and reusable datasets. Bradley Terry fits fixed model strengths better than sequential Elo.

  • Finding: Adopted benchmarks align with human preferences, separate models with confidence, and use fresh prompts.

1. Origin

Arena began as a response to a credibility problem. The team trained Vicuna-13B by fine-tuning LLaMA on 70,000 user-shared conversations collected through ShareGPT and built FastChat as an open-source toolkit for training and evaluating chat models.

Early evaluation relied on GPT-4 as a judge, but a single automated score was not persuasive enough to establish that Vicuna performed better. Arena introduced direct, pairwise model comparisons based on human votes.

Why It Gained Traction

  • Competition among proprietary and open-source models was intense, and many early voters were developers.

  • Users could access GPT-4, Claude, and PaLM 2 for free inside the arena.

  • The team published an updated leaderboard every two weeks.

  • The MT-Bench paper gave the evaluation method research visibility.

  • Open datasets made the system useful beyond the product itself.

2. Ranking System

Elo

Arena initially used Elo because it was familiar and had already appeared in Anthropic’s LLM research.

E_A = 1 / (1 + 10^((R_B − R_A) / 400))

R_A′ = R_A + K · (S_A − E_A)

Elo updates ratings one comparison at a time, so results depend on vote order and the selected K value. That behavior makes sense for chess players whose skill changes, but models remain fixed during evaluation.

Bradley Terry

P(A beats B) = 1 / (1 + e^(ξ_B − ξ_A))

  • Each model receives one fitted strength value, ξ.

  • All votes are fitted together through logistic regression.

  • Each battle becomes one row, with +1 for model A and −1 for model B.

  • A tie counts as half a win and half a loss.

  • The fitted strength is rescaled to resemble Elo, making a 100-point difference roughly equivalent to a 64% win probability.

Potential Upgrades

  • Davidson / Rao Kupper: Model ties directly instead of converting them into partial wins and losses.

  • Crowd-BT: Weight voters according to their estimated reliability.

  • Prompt-to-Leaderboard: Estimate model rankings conditionally for different kinds of prompts.

  • Mixture Models: Represent different user preferences instead of forcing every vote into one shared ranking.

3. Arena-Hard

A stronger benchmark depends on three qualities:

  • Human Agreement: Scores should correlate with human preferences in real-world use cases.

  • Separability: Scores should include confidence intervals and distinguish models with high confidence.

  • Freshness: Prompts should be new and unseen to reduce test leakage.

Read the Arena-Hard blog or visit the GitHub repository.

IDEP · Research notes

Original blog post

from-ai-creativity-to-3d-agents.title: From AI Creativity to 3D Agents
from-ai-creativity-to-3d-agents.body:
03 · Interview synthesis

TL;DR

  • Why: We interviewed creativity researchers to clarify what should be measured and what evidence matters.

  • Key points: Creativity evaluation must separate outcome, behavior, and process. A strategy should work within its environment, differ in its logic, and create value over time.

  • Finding: 3D simulation can reveal how a strategy emerges and whether it transfers across changing environments.

1. Define

The interviews revealed that AI creativity research often examines different objects.

  • Cheng Qian: In EscapeBench and CreativityBench, creativity appears as unconventional but effective tool use within a constrained action space.

  • Antonios Liapis: Creativity cannot be reduced to a final artifact. It emerges through interaction, selection, and shifts in direction.

  • Vijeta Deshpande: A shared capability appears across creativity tasks, but it cannot explain why an output matters in a specific context.

These different definitions also lead researchers to evaluate creativity at different levels.

  • Outcome: Task completion, novelty, and usefulness. Easy to compare; weak at explaining how a solution emerged.

  • Behavior: Tools used and strategy selected. Reveals meaningful difference, but may mistake randomness for exploration.

  • Process: Departure from the common path, response to failure, and triggers for strategy shifts. Shows how ideas evolve and influence later decisions.

These levels answer three different questions: what result was produced, what method was used, and how that method was discovered.

2. Reframe

Moving away from a universal creativity score does not mean discarding the earlier research. The interviews helped us preserve three forms of evidence that can travel across domains:

  • Outcome: Whether the agent solved the problem and whether the result was effective and reproducible.

  • Process: How the agent explored, failed, gathered information, and changed direction, including whether an early attempt became valuable later.

  • Strategy: Which approach the agent ultimately used and whether it truly differed from the common solution.

Using this evidence, we can replace the broad judgment “Is this behavior creative?” with three more specific judgments: Does it work within the environmental constraints? Does its strategic logic differ? Does it create value over time?

3. Ground

Qiancheng’s research provides a key bridge. In EscapeBench, an agent completes escape-room-like tasks using available objects and actions. Success remains objectively verifiable, but the correct intermediate steps are not prescribed.

CreativityBench extends this idea to unconventional object use. Together, the benchmarks combine a clear goal with an open solution space where behavior leaves verifiable consequences.

In 3D simulation, agents act through spatial relationships and environmental feedback. Researchers can replay complete trajectories and systematically vary the world.

The shift. Qiancheng’s work asks whether an agent can find an unconventional but effective solution; 3D simulation lets us ask how that solution emerged and whether it transfers.

IDEP · Research notes

Original blog post

simulation-in-3d-worlds.title: Simulation in 3D Worlds
simulation-in-3d-worlds.body:
04 · Current direction

TL;DR

  • Why: We needed to identify where 3D simulation creates value beyond interviews, spreadsheets, and conventional simulation.

  • Key points: Behavioral simulation predicts coordination. Physical simulation tests action with spatial consequences. The two directions are high stakes collective orchestration and embodied task execution.

  • Finding: We should choose one focused vertical where 3D is essential, potentially a task in the home.

1. Distinguish

Simulating agent-to-agent communication in a three-dimensional setting is different from placing agents inside a world governed by physical properties.

  • Behavioral Simulation: Models how people or agents communicate, coordinate, and make decisions inside a spatial context.

  • Physical Simulation: Models movement, object interaction, spatial constraints, and embodied task execution, as required in robotics.

The first predicts behavior. The second tests whether an agent can act successfully in a world with physical consequences. Our next decision is which of these systems creates a meaningful and testable form of enterprise value.

The Simile Reference

Simile applies behavioral prediction to retail and merchandising contexts, including work associated with CVS. Its direction moved away from a persistent 3D environment and toward collecting richer human-behavior data through interviews.

When does representing behavior in 3D add value that cannot be produced through interviews, spreadsheets, or conventional simulation?

2. Orchestrate

One direction is large-scale orchestration: using simulation to compare plans before many people must execute them under time pressure.

The useful cases share three properties: many people, a short execution window, and a high cost of failure.

  • Retail: Coordinate merchandising, staffing, customer flow, and operational changes across a store.

  • Plant Turnaround: Plan maintenance logistics when a refinery or industrial plant must stop, service equipment, and restart quickly.

  • Hospital Move Day: Coordinate staff, patients, equipment, routes, and dependencies during a facility transition.

  • Architecture Planning: Test how layouts influence movement, collaboration, congestion, and use before construction or reconfiguration.

3. Embody

A second direction is to simulate physical environments and evaluate how agents manipulate objects, navigate constraints, and discover effective strategies.

  • Generated Homes: Create diverse 3D domestic environments for training and evaluating robots on household tasks.

  • Drone Airspace: Simulate traffic, separation, and detect-and-avoid behavior for operations beyond the pilot’s visual line of sight.

The FAA has proposed Part 108 as a framework for routine beyond-visual-line-of-sight operations. This creates a timely setting for testing how autonomous systems detect aircraft, respond to conflict, and coordinate safely in shared airspace.

Read the FAA proposed BVLOS rule.

Open decision. Simulate collective behavior, or test embodied task execution?

IDEP · Research notes

Original blog post

human-evaluation-needed-for-physical-ai.title: Human Evaluation Needed for Physical AI
human-evaluation-needed-for-physical-ai.body:
How physical AI is evaluated

A useful starting map separates four sources of evaluation evidence, plus approaches that combine them. These categories overlap; they are not an exhaustive list of benchmarks.

Method What supplies the evidence What it tells us and what still needs checking
Programmed checks and task metrics Goal conditions, environment state and measured outcomes. Tests whether a task was completed and how efficiently. BEHAVIOR uses logical goal conditions and progress metrics; Habitat includes success weighted by path length. Human experience requires additional measures.
Comparison with reference data Verified answers, physical measurements or human demonstrations. Tests performance against a known reference. BEHAVIOR compares efficiency with human demonstrators. Similarity to a reference does not by itself establish that a different, valid strategy is inappropriate.
Model based judging An LLM reading a description or action record, or a vision language model examining images or video. Can estimate progress, success or rubric scores. RoboReward studies VLM reward models on robot tasks and finds that no evaluated model excels across all tasks. A model’s judgment needs validation for the target setting.
Human evaluation Expert review, observer ratings, pairwise preferences, interviews or feedback from people interacting with the robot. Can examine comfort, predictability, timing and social appropriateness. Who participates and whether they observe or experience an encounter affect what the evidence represents.
Hybrid evaluation Automated scores checked or corrected using sampled human judgments. Can combine scale with a human reference. Prediction powered inference offers a statistical approach in language model evaluation; whether it works well for our physical AI encounters remains a question to test.

The programmed and reference based examples come from BEHAVIOR and Habitat’s SPL metric. The model judging example is RoboReward.

Human experience is already part of social robotics research. Principles and Guidelines for Evaluating Social Robot Navigation Algorithms includes comfort, legibility, politeness and responsiveness to context alongside safety. Research on simulation and interactivity also examines how the evaluation setting affects perceptions. The hybrid example comes from Stratified Prediction Powered Inference, which does not establish transfer to physical AI.

The setting is a separate choice

These methods can be used in different settings: recorded datasets, simulated worlds, controlled real robot trials or deployed environments. Simulation is a place to run an evaluation; it does not determine who judges the result. A simulated encounter could be scored by programmed rules, a model, a person or a combination.

What we want to understand next

Our working hypothesis is that human judgment adds information about how an agent behaves around people, beyond whether it finishes a task. For IDEP, the question is how to collect that information consistently, connect it to specific actions, and test whether automated judges can predict it.

The next question: when two agents both complete the same task, what makes people prefer one encounter over the other?
